A1-A2.headline: The Story Of A Famous Old English Paper

pages.text:
Can a king make all the rules by himself? In England, many powerful men were unhappy with King John. In 1215, they met him at Runnymede and asked him to agree to new rules.

A paper was made official with the king's great seal. It later became known as Magna Carta. The paper was an attempt to make peace and limit some of the king's power.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound. (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

pages.text:
The picture shows King John with the charter, but it was made long after the meeting. People did not need the king's written name on the paper. His great seal was used to make it official.

The agreement did not end the trouble. The king and the men who opposed him went to war. The first charter did not bring lasting peace.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text:
After John died, his young son Henry III became king. The people who ran his government brought back the charter in 1216. They took out some of its stronger rules and tried to win support.

There were later versions too. This old picture of the first charter helps us see how a written agreement could outlive the king who made it.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
A paper can have different meanings at different times. When the charter first appeared, it was about the problems of England in the Middle Ages. The men who had a lot of land wanted to protect their rights. The paper did not give the same rights to every person in the country. Later kings agreed to new versions of it. Sometimes they did this when they needed money.

Many years later, people began to read the old charter in a new way. They thought it showed that England had a long history of freedom. Lawyers used it when they talked about the power of kings. Their ideas about the past were not always right. These ideas led to arguments about power. But the old paper became useful in new arguments about rights and the law.

The story of Magna Carta did not end in England. People in America also learned about the charter and the ideas that had grown around it. They used some of those ideas when they thought about laws and government. The paper itself was very old, but the questions it raised were still important. How much power should a leader have? What can people do when power is used unfairly?

Today, only a small part of the old charter is still part of English law. Most of its rules no longer apply. Yet people continue to care about the document. Copies can be seen and studied. The charter is a well-known sign of the idea that even a powerful ruler must live under the law. Its history helps us understand why that idea matters.

B1-B2.headline: How A Medieval Charter Shaped Modern Democracy And Liberty

pages.text:
In 1215, King John faced opposition from powerful English barons. They wanted protection against the way he exercised royal authority. At Runnymede, a royal charter offered a possible way out of the crisis.

The document, now known as Magna Carta, tried to settle a political conflict through written commitments rather than continued fighting.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound. (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

pages.text:
A later illustration imagines the meeting between John and the barons. The original charter was authenticated with the royal seal, rather than a handwritten signature from the king.

The agreement soon collapsed. Its annulment and the conflict that followed show that a written promise could not by itself resolve the political crisis.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text:
The government of the young Henry III reissued the charter in 1216, removing some of its most radical provisions. The changes helped make it a more useful political settlement.

Further versions followed, and the charter became part of English public life. The engraving preserves the appearance of a document from the first attempt.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
Magna Carta's practical importance changed over the centuries. Kings confirmed later versions of the charter, sometimes in exchange for agreement to taxation. The document became connected with the relationship between royal government and those whose support it needed. Its original setting was a medieval society in which rights and obligations were not shared equally among all people.

By the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, lawyers and historians were interpreting the charter in a different way. They saw it as evidence of ancient English liberties and drew on it in debates about royal power. Later historical research challenged this interpretation, but the political influence of the charter was not limited by the accuracy of the earlier account.

The charter's reputation extended beyond its original legal purpose. Ideas associated with Magna Carta travelled to the American colonies and influenced later constitutional thinking. The distinction between the medieval text and the principles that later readers drew from it matters: a document created to manage a particular conflict acquired a much wider symbolic role.

Today, most of the charter's provisions have been repealed. Its survival in public memory does not mean that the original agreement established modern democracy. Rather, successive generations adapted its meaning as they debated the limits of government. Its lasting appeal is linked to the principle that the exercise of power should be subject to law, not simply the wishes of a ruler.

C1-C2.headline: The Enduring Legacy Of Magna Carta In Global Constitutional History

pages.text:
The confrontation at Runnymede in 1215 exposed tensions between royal authority and the interests of the English baronage. The charter offered a negotiated framework for constraining aspects of John's rule.

Its immediate objective was a political settlement, not the creation of a modern constitution or a comprehensive system of individual rights.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound. (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

pages.text:
The familiar nineteenth-century depiction of John signing the charter retrospectively dramatizes the encounter. Authentication in 1215 depended on the royal seal rather than the monarch's signature.

The settlement's rapid collapse reveals the gulf between formally articulated obligations and the political conditions required to enforce them.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text:
The regency of Henry III revived the charter in 1216, omitting some of its more contentious provisions. Subsequent reissues embedded the document in changing relationships between the Crown and its subjects.

The engraving of the 1215 text recalls the original settlement, which should be distinguished from the later versions that acquired legal force.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
Magna Carta's subsequent significance cannot be deduced solely from its original provisions. Reconfirmations, often associated with fiscal concessions, situated the charter within the evolving political relationship between the monarchy and the communities from which it sought resources. By the late sixteenth century, a renewed interest in English legal history encouraged interpretations that attributed much broader significance to the document.

Jurists subsequently invoked the charter as evidence of supposedly ancient liberties when challenging expansive claims to royal prerogative. Later scholarship exposed the limitations of that historical narrative. The episode illustrates how a historically questionable interpretation can nonetheless acquire substantial political influence.

The transatlantic reception of Magna Carta further complicated the relationship between textual meaning and constitutional legacy. Its influence on American legal thought was mediated by interpretations that extended well beyond the immediate concerns of the medieval baronage. Accordingly, the charter's historical function and its later symbolic resonance should not be conflated.

The survival of only a limited number of its provisions in English law does not diminish the importance of this distinction. Its contemporary status rests less on the continued application of the original settlement than on the accumulated authority of successive readings. The enduring appeal of the charter lies in the possibility of subordinating the exercise of political power to legal constraints.
